paragraphs.text: This red tea comes from [Yuchi](yuchi:where-it-is), the township around Sun Moon Lake in the middle of Nantou County, where tea grows on gentle slopes at roughly 600 to 800 metres. The basin is warm and misty, with deep reddish soil, and the Japanese tea men who first trialled it compared it to [the Assam country of India](yuchi:why-red-tea). Under Japanese rule, large leaf [Assam seed brought from India](yuchi:assam-planting) was planted here to make red tea for export. This leaf was made in 1977, while that trade was [fading](yuchi:decline-and-return): from the 1970s, rising wages made hand picked leaf costly against red tea from other countries, and many growers in the township turned to oolong or to other crops.

[Red tea](red:definition), the fully oxidised tea that English calls black tea, has [no tradition of ageing](red:ageing). Sealed, it is expected to keep its quality for a year and a half to three years. This leaf has been kept for forty-nine years, long past that span.

brewing.text: Red tea takes water near the boil, about 90 to 100°C; hotter water draws out its aroma and flavour more fully, but its bitterness faster too. In a pot or mug, use about a rounded spoon of leaf for each cup and steep three to five minutes, less for broken leaf and a little less, and a little cooler, for a light, delicate tea. Left too long, it turns bitter and drying, because time and heat pull more tannins from the leaf.

notice.text: A sweet cup, often with honey, floral or fruity notes, malt in many, and a brisk strength in the stronger teas. The liquor runs red, bright to deep.
